W.01.stem: Based on the weaknesses of absolutism described in the passage, what would most likely happen to an absolute monarchy inherited by a weak or reckless ruler?

choices.text: The whole state could be endangered because so much power depended on that one ruler
An elected assembly would immediately remove the ruler from power
The nobility would gain a legal right to overrule the monarch
Power would automatically divide itself among several branches of government

remediation.B: Reteach that an absolute monarchy had no assembly able to vote out the ruler.
remediation.C: Reteach that absolutism gave nobles no legal power to overrule the monarch.
remediation.D: Reteach that separated branches of government describe a limited system, not an absolute monarchy.

W.02.stem: A student argues that by 1700 England and France had taken 'opposite paths.' Which statement best supports this claim?

choices.text: Both expanded royal power equally during the 1600s
England limited the monarch by law while France concentrated power in one ruler
Both abolished their monarchies before 1700
Neither country had a law-making body

remediation.A: Reteach the contrast: England limited royal power by law while France under Louis XIV concentrated it, so their paths diverged.
remediation.C: Reteach that both kept a monarch; England's became limited (constitutional) while France's stayed absolute.
remediation.D: Reteach that England's Parliament was a law-making body whose power grew as the monarch's shrank.

W.03.stem: Hobbes and Locke most clearly disagreed about which question?

choices.text: Whether reason could be used to study government
Whether trade should be permitted
Whether people are best served by an all-powerful ruler or by a government that can be replaced
Whether kings ruled by the divine right of God

remediation.A: Reteach that both thinkers applied reason; their split was over a strong ruler (Hobbes) versus a replaceable government (Locke).
remediation.B: Reteach that the Hobbes/Locke disagreement was about the kind of government people need, not trade.
remediation.D: Reteach that both reasoned about government; Hobbes favored a strong ruler while Locke said the people may replace a failing government.

W.04.stem: Why was the 1649 execution of Charles I considered a turning point in ideas about kingship?

choices.text: It proved that kings truly ruled by divine right
It brought an end to all warfare in Europe
It made Oliver Cromwell the new king of England
It showed that even a king could be held accountable by his own subjects

remediation.A: Reteach that the trial and execution undercut the idea that a king was untouchable.
remediation.B: Reteach that the execution did not end warfare across Europe.
remediation.C: Reteach that Cromwell led a republic, the Commonwealth, and did not become king.

W.08a.stem: A historian claims the Declaration shows 'an idea moving from a philosopher's page to the founding of a nation.' Which evidence best supports this claim?

choices.text: Jefferson wrote the Declaration without reading any Enlightenment works
The Declaration avoids any mention of rights
Locke's natural-rights argument reappears as Jefferson's 'unalienable Rights'
The Declaration defends the divine right of kings

remediation.A: Reteach that Jefferson borrowed directly from Enlightenment thinkers.
remediation.B: Reteach that rights are the core of the Declaration's argument.
remediation.D: Reteach that the Declaration opposed divine right.
